## What spectral tilt measures

Many acoustic measures describe how a voice's energy is distributed across the
spectrum. One family compares the amplitude of the first harmonic with a later
harmonic or a formant: H1 against H2 gives H1–H2, and H1 against the first or
third formant gives H1–A1 and H1–A3 [@kreiman2011foundations]. What they share
is the observation that weakness and breathiness go with less high-frequency
energy in the voice [@kreiman2011foundations].

## H1–H2

### Definition

H1–H2 is the difference in amplitude between the first harmonic (H1) and the
second harmonic (H2) of the voice spectrum, in decibels
[@kreiman2011foundations; @toles2025pressed]. It indirectly measures the
relative length of the open phase of glottal oscillation
[@barsties2018meta; @delgado2018avqi]. In breathy voices the first harmonic is
relatively strong compared with the weaker harmonics that follow it
[@barsties2018meta; @delgado2018avqi], so increasing weakness or breathiness
generally raises H1–H2 [@kreiman2011foundations]. Lower values are taken to
reflect greater glottal closure, and higher values less vocal fold adduction
[@toles2025pressed]. That reading is an assumption in the literature, and the
evidence below tests it.

H1–H2 is also one of the nine components of the
[Acoustic Breathiness Index](abi.qmd) [@barsties2017abi].

### How it is computed

The formula is trivial:

$$
\text{H1–H2} = A(\text{H1}) - A(\text{H2}) \quad \text{[dB]}
$$

Everything that makes two H1–H2 values comparable lies outside it: how the
first harmonic is found, which spectrum its amplitude is read from, over what
stretch of signal, and whether the harmonic amplitudes are corrected for the
formants of the vowel. The sources in this reference compute it in at least
three different ways, and they are not interchangeable.

| Implementation | Harmonic location | Spectrum | Averaging | Formant correction | Stated in full? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ABI script [@barsties2017abi] | F0 from the cepstral peak (60–400 Hz search); H1 = spectral maximum within ±20 Hz of it; H2 within ±20 Hz of twice that frequency | LTAS of each window, 6-Hz bandwidth | consecutive 0.1-s windows of the concatenated speech-and-vowel signal, then the mean | none | yes |
| PhonaLab [@lucero2026subsets] | computed as one of the ABI components | — | — | — | engine stated: Parselmouth 0.4.7 (Praat 6.1.38) |
| Toles laboratory [@toles2025pressed; @toles2026kinematics] | not stated | not stated | not stated | not stated | no: a custom script ("Phonanium CommV") |
| Fröhlich et al. [@frohlich2000breathiness] | two forms: a peak-level and a regional-level difference | short-time power spectrum | not stated here | not stated here | partly |

: Implementations of H1–H2 in the sources of this chapter. {#tbl-h1h2-variants}

Two details of the ABI script deserve attention. Its own comment says the
signal is cut into 0.05-s portions, but the code sets the window to 0.1 s, and
the code is what runs. And it reads H1 and H2 from the uncorrected spectrum:
there is no step that compensates for a formant lying near either harmonic.

Toles and Murton note that H1–H2 is missing from commercial packages such as
ADSV, and that it can be computed in Praat [@toles2025pressed].

### Reference values

::: {.callout-important}
**No reference value for H1–H2 exists in the sources of this reference.** There
is no normative range for typical voices, on sustained vowels or connected
speech, and no diagnostic cutoff.
:::

| Population | Task | Value | Pipeline | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adults with typical voice | Sustained vowel | No published reference in the sources reviewed | — | — |
| Adults with typical voice | Connected speech | No published reference in the sources reviewed | — | — |
| Voice disorder vs. typical voice | Any | No published cutoff in the sources reviewed | — | — |

: H1–H2 reference values: declared absence. {#tbl-h1h2-reference}

The only typical-voice means available come from a study of simulated
phonation types in healthy speakers, computed with a script whose method is
not stated [@toles2025pressed]. They appear in @fig-h1h2-phonation and under
[Confounds and cautions](#sec-h1h2-cautions) as descriptive values, classed
`unclassified (pipeline not stated)`. They are not a normal range. The
correlations, odds ratios and AUCs reported below are performance metrics, not
reference values.

### What it captures

**Breathiness, on sustained vowels.** In the 2018 meta-analysis of acoustic
correlates of roughness and breathiness, H1–H2 reached a pooled effect size of
*r*~w~ = .66 (N = 248) for breathiness, from four studies on different
sustained vowels in healthy and pathological speakers [@barsties2018meta]. It
was one of the twelve measures the authors named as the most promising
predictors of breathiness [@barsties2018meta]. The ABI development study found
almost no relationship in its own data; see
[Where the sources disagree](#sec-h1h2-disagreement).

**Breathiness, in connected speech.** Only one study tested it, with
*r* = −.57 and N = 16, among the single-study measures below the
meta-analysis's .60 threshold [@barsties2018meta]. The appendix lists the
negative sign without comment.

**Pressed and breathy phonation.** Toles and Murton recorded 50 vocally healthy
adults producing sustained /ɑ/, /i/ and /u/ and an all-voiced sentence in
typical, pressed and breathy phonation [@toles2025pressed]. On the sentence,
H1–H2 differed among all three: higher in breathy and lower in pressed
phonation, with means of 8.3, 2.3 and 0.6 dB [@toles2025pressed]. On sustained
vowels the picture depends on sex. Women had lower H1–H2 in pressed than in
typical phonation, but higher H1–H2 in breathy phonation only on /ɑ/. Men
showed no difference between pressed and typical phonation on any vowel
[@toles2025pressed].

```{python}
#| label: fig-h1h2-phonation
#| fig-cap: "Mean H1–H2 (± 1 SD) by task and phonation type, in 36 women and 14 men (by sex assigned at birth) simulating typical, breathy and pressed phonation. Data from Table 2 of @toles2025pressed. In women the means are ordered on every task, breathy highest and pressed lowest, although breathy and typical phonation differed significantly only on /ɑ/. In men, pressed and typical phonation overlap on every sustained vowel and separate only on the sentence. Note also the scale of the sex difference in typical phonation on /i/ and /u/. These are descriptive means from simulated phonation in healthy speakers, computed with a script whose method is not stated: unclassified (pipeline not stated), and not reference values."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels, women on the left and men on the right. Each shows four tasks on the horizontal axis (sentence, /ɑ/, /i/, /u/) and mean H1–H2 in decibels on the vertical axis, with three markers per task for breathy, typical and pressed phonation and vertical bars for one standard deviation. In the women's panel breathy is highest and pressed lowest on every task. In the men's panel breathy is highest, while typical and pressed nearly coincide on the three vowels."

tasks = ["Sentence", "/ɑ/", "/i/", "/u/"]
# Table 2 of Toles & Murton (2025): mean (SD), dB. Order: breathy, typical, pressed.
data = {
    "Women (n = 36)": {
        "Breathy": [(9.0, 5.5), (12.8, 4.4), (14.2, 6.1), (11.5, 4.6)],
        "Typical": [(2.7, 3.9), (8.5, 3.6), (13.3, 5.4), (9.4, 5.5)],
        "Pressed": [(0.8, 3.5), (5.3, 3.1), (8.9, 6.4), (4.5, 6.0)],
    },
    "Men (n = 14)": {
        "Breathy": [(6.4, 3.1), (9.1, 4.1), (7.7, 5.5), (7.4, 3.9)],
        "Typical": [(1.6, 2.6), (4.9, 3.1), (0.1, 3.6), (0.4, 3.5)],
        "Pressed": [(-0.2, 2.2), (4.0, 2.6), (1.0, 5.6), (-0.7, 3.4)],
    },
}
style = {"Breathy": (vs.BLUE, "o", -0.18),
         "Typical": (vs.INK, "s", 0.0),
         "Pressed": (vs.ORANGE, "D", 0.18)}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.5), sharey=True)
x = np.arange(len(tasks))
for ax, (panel, groups) in zip(axes, data.items()):
    for cond, rows in groups.items():
        c, m, dx = style[cond]
        mu = np.array([r[0] for r in rows]); sd = np.array([r[1] for r in rows])
        ax.errorbar(x + dx, mu, yerr=sd, fmt=m, ms=5, color=c, ecolor=c,
                    elinewidth=1.0, capsize=2.5, markeredgecolor="white",
                    markeredgewidth=0.6, zorder=3)
    ax.axhline(0, color=vs.MUTED, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    ax.set_xticks(x, tasks)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(tasks) - 0.5)
    ax.set_title(panel)
    vs.style_axes(ax)
axes[0].set_ylabel("H1–H2  [dB]")
handles = [Line2D([], [], marker=style[k][1], ls="", ms=5, color=style[k][0],
                  label=k) for k in ("Breathy", "Typical", "Pressed")]
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False,
           fontsize=8, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02))
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
```

**Telling the phonation types apart.** The study tested discrimination with
logistic models at a significance level of 0.0125 [@toles2025pressed]. H1–H2
separated pressed from typical phonation on /ɑ/ (*P* = 0.005) and /u/
(*P* = 0.003), but not on the sentence (*P* = 0.027) or /i/ (*P* = 0.103)
[@toles2025pressed]. Its AUCs were 0.62 to 0.75 for pressed against typical
phonation, and 0.64 to 0.86 for breathy against typical [@toles2025pressed].
For breathy phonation, each 1-dB increase in H1–H2 raised the odds of breathy
phonation by 11% to 48% across tasks, and intensity did not contribute
significantly to those models [@toles2025pressed].

**Glottal closure, seen directly.** A later study from the same group recorded
40 healthy adults with high-speed videoendoscopy while they sustained /i:/ in
the three phonation types [@toles2026kinematics]. H1–H2 rose with the closing
quotient (*r* = .53), the share of the cycle spent closing, and with the
amplitude-to-length ratio (*r* = .40). It fell as closure became faster and
more abrupt: *r* = −.56 with the normalized maximum area declination rate,
−.40 with the speed index and −.61 with the stiffness index
[@toles2026kinematics]. The relationships with the three closure-speed
measures were strong in breathy phonation and small or negligible in pressed
phonation; only the closing-quotient relationship held across all three
phonation types [@toles2026kinematics]. The authors suggest that
hyperadduction may introduce nonlinear source–filter interaction that hides
the kinematics from the acoustic signal [@toles2026kinematics].

**Roughness and strain in a clinical database.** In 288 recordings from the
Perceptual Voice Qualities Database, H1–H2 entered the best subset for CAPE-V
roughness with a coefficient of β = −0.43 and the best subset for CAPE-V
strain with β = −0.52 [@lucero2026subsets]. These are coefficients in
multivariable regression models, not simple correlations. In a QR
factorization with column pivoting, F0 and H1–H2 were pivoted first among 14
parameters, which the paper reads as contributing the most linearly
independent information [@lucero2026subsets]. The paper reads the roughness
coefficient as irregular vibration producing a flatter spectral envelope
[@lucero2026subsets]. That study was written by this reference's author.

**A low value is not specific.** Lower H1–H2 accompanies simulated pressed
phonation [@toles2025pressed], and in the database models it also accompanies
higher roughness and higher strain ratings [@lucero2026subsets]. A low H1–H2
on its own does not say which of these is present. That is this reference's
reading of the two sources together, not a finding of either.

### Confounds and cautions {#sec-h1h2-cautions}

**Implementation.** The variants in @tbl-h1h2-variants differ in how they
locate the harmonics, in spectral resolution and in averaging, and one does
not state its method at all. No study in this reference compares H1–H2 across
implementations on the same recordings. Do not compare an H1–H2 value with one
from another implementation.

**Speech task.** In the same 50 typical speakers, mean H1–H2 in typical
phonation was 2.3 dB on the sentence and 7.5, 9.6 and 6.9 dB on sustained /ɑ/,
/i/ and /u/ [@toles2025pressed]. A value means little without its task.

**Sex.** On sustained vowels in typical phonation, women's means were 8.5,
13.3 and 9.4 dB on /ɑ/, /i/ and /u/, against 4.9, 0.1 and 0.4 dB in men
[@toles2025pressed]. On the sentence the two were close, 2.7 and 1.6 dB
[@toles2025pressed]. On vowels the sex difference is as large as the
phonation-type effects, so an H1–H2 value read without the speaker's sex is not
interpretable. No source in this reference explains why the difference is so
large on /i/ and /u/. For the pressed-phonation effect, Toles and Murton point
to the small posterior glottal gap common in women during typical phonation,
which pressing can close. Men's typical phonation usually has complete closure
already, so there is less to change [@toles2025pressed].

**Sign and range.** H1–H2 can be negative. Men's mean on the sentence in
pressed phonation was −0.2 dB [@toles2025pressed]. Across 288 database
recordings the mean was 4.20 dB, with SD 6.14 dB and a range from −20.62 to
25.15 dB, which is why it was analysed untransformed [@lucero2026subsets].

**Simulated phonation in healthy speakers.** The phonation-type findings come
from healthy speakers imitating pressed and breathy voice, and may not
generalize to people with voice disorders [@toles2026kinematics]. A single
blinded voice-specialized speech-language pathologist rated the productions in
the 2025 study and identified the nonmodal phonation correctly 96% of the time
[@toles2025pressed]. The 2026 recordings were made during rigid transoral
endoscopy, with the posture and tongue position that requires
[@toles2026kinematics].

**Two studies, probably one cohort.** The two Toles studies share a laboratory,
an ethics protocol and a recording chain, and report the same enrolment and
exclusion counts [@toles2025pressed; @toles2026kinematics]. They very probably
draw on largely the same speakers. They are therefore not independent
confirmations of each other. This is this reference's inference; neither paper
states it.

**Language.** In some languages phonation type is contrastive, and H1–H2
carries the contrast. Breathy vowels in Hmong differ from modal vowels in
H1–H2, and laryngealization in Mixtec lowers it [@kreiman2011foundations].
Green Mong vowels can be sorted correctly 92% of the time from H1–H2,
duration, F0, jitter and shimmer, with H1–H2 doing most of the work
[@kreiman2011foundations]. In such a language a clinical reading of H1–H2 has
to allow for the linguistic contrast.

### Where the sources disagree {#sec-h1h2-disagreement}

**How strongly H1–H2 tracks breathiness.** The meta-analysis reports
*r*~w~ = .66 on sustained vowels [@barsties2018meta]. In the ABI development
study, H1–H2 correlated with breathiness ratings at only *r*~s~ = 0.098 on
1042 concatenated Dutch speech-and-vowel samples, one of the weakest of the
candidate measures [@barsties2017abi]. It was kept in the index all the same,
on the strength of its earlier record as a breathiness predictor
[@barsties2017abi]. The two figures differ in task, sample and pipeline, and
neither source reconciles them. This chapter reports both.

**What the phonation-type study shows.** Toles and Murton's discussion calls
H1–H2 the only variable significant for pressed phonation in both sustained
vowels and connected speech [@toles2025pressed]. Their own table gives
*P* = 0.027 on the sentence and *P* = 0.103 on /i/, against their stated
significance level of 0.0125, and their abstract correctly reports that
neither measure separated pressed from typical phonation on /i/
[@toles2025pressed]. This chapter follows the table.

### Validation

The perceptual evidence for H1–H2 is the breathiness meta-analysis
[@barsties2018meta] and the index development study that included it
[@barsties2017abi], and the two disagree about its strength. The physiological
evidence is two studies of simulated phonation in healthy adults from one
laboratory, one acoustic [@toles2025pressed] and one with simultaneous
high-speed imaging [@toles2026kinematics]. A database analysis places it in
the roughness and strain subsets [@lucero2026subsets]. What is still missing
is any H1–H2 reference computed with a stated pipeline, and any comparison
between implementations. Until one exists, this chapter publishes no H1–H2
normal range.
